entries.title: White Sox-Cardinals series opener delayed by rain
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS, Mo. — The start of Friday's series opener between the White Sox and Cardinals will be delayed by inclement weather. </p><p>Originally scheduled for a 7:15pm CT first pitch, the Cardinals grounds crew put the tarp on the field shortly after 6 p.m., and the skies opened up a few minutes later. While the tarp has since been pulled, the Cardinals announced that the start of the game will be delayed, and have yet to provide a new first pitch time.</p><p>While the matchup between left-handers Anthony Kay and Matthew Liberatore will be delayed, the weather had minimal effect on a pregame ceremony honoring the 20th anniversary of the 2006 World Series-winning Cardinals team. Former White Sox manager Tony La Russa, who managed that Cardinals club, was among the honorees, alongside franchise legends Albert Pujols and Yadier Molina.</p><p>White Sox first baseman Munetaka Murakami is out of the starting lineup Friday night, as manager Will Venable is attempting to provide one last "rest" day for each positional regular before the close of the season. Miguel Vargas was the recipient of such a "day off" on Wednesday, but wound up pinch-hitting in the sixth and playing the rest of the game. Murakami's night out of the lineup could easily follow the same template.</p>

entries.title: Chicago Grammy-winning rapper Lil Durk acquitted by federal jury in murder-for-hire case
entries.summary: <p>A federal jury on Friday found rapper <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/lil-durk-florida-indicted-los-angeles-5d55866b2caf5ef5bd7d3cef43b6ced8" target="_blank" >Lil Durk</a> not guilty of the attempted killing for hire of rival rapper <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/rapper-quando-rondo-guilty-plea-drugs-4b34f818ded78d3fc1e58c8a41a3a28f" target="_blank" >Quando Rondo</a> at a Los Angeles gas station, a shooting that resulted in the death of Rondo’s cousin.</p><p>The jury deliberated for three days before acquitting Lil Durk, the 33-year-old Grammy-winning Chicago hip-hop artist best known for the 2023 hit “All My Life,” of conspiracy, stalking resulting in death and murder for hire.</p><p>Durk supporters including music stars <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/machine-gun-kelly" target="_blank" >Machine Gun Kelly</a> and Ye — the artist formerly known as <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/kanye-west" target="_blank" >Kanye West</a> — appeared in the audience during the two-week trial in downtown Los Angeles. Big groups of fans, livestreamers and other content creators gathered outside the courthouse.</p><p>Durk’s co-defendants Deandre Wilson and David Lindsey were convicted of conspiracy to commit stalking, stalking using a dangerous weapon and stalking resulting in death. But both were also acquitted of murder for hire.</p><p>“We thank the jury for seeing there was no murder for hire,” Wilson's attorney Craig Harbaugh said in an email. “We are confident the remaining counts will not survive our pending motion for acquittal.”</p><p>Attorneys for Durk and Lindsey did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment.</p><p>Durk, whose legal name is Durk Banks, remained in custody, pending a forthcoming trial on a racketeering count that was severed from this trial. He has been jailed since his 2024 arrest.</p><p>Prosecutors had alleged that Durk paid to have Rondo killed after someone from Rondo’s entourage fatally shot rapper King Von, a close friend of Durk's and a member of his Only The Family hip-hop collective, at an Atlanta nightclub in 2020.</p><p>The prosecution alleged that in August 2022, a group of men flew to Los Angeles with funds provided by Durk, followed Rondo and his crew around, and three gunmen fired on his Escalade near the Beverly Center shopping mall in Los Angeles. Rondo survived, but his 24-year-old cousin, Saviay’a Robinson, known as Lul Pab, was killed.</p><p>“Today, the jury delivered justice to the family of Saviay’a Robinson, finding defendants Deandre Wilson and David Lindsey guilty of stalking resulting in Mr. Robinson’s death," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement. “While we are disappointed with the jury’s decision regarding Durk Banks, a.k.a. ‘Lil Durk,’ we look forward to presenting our evidence at his second trial."</p><p>Durk won a Grammy earlier that year for Best Melodic Rap Performance for “All My Life,” which features J. Cole. He has been nominated for three other Grammys and was a featured performer on Drake’s “Laugh Now Cry Later.”</p>

entries.title: Young White Sox still 'feel like we are the best team in the division' ahead of crucial stretch
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS, Mo. — From a detached, outsider perspective, the 2026 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> have been doing backstrokes in an infinity pool full of house money all year. To have 75 wins at all, let alone with 16 games remaining, is already beating most of their preseason projections.</p><p>From a clubhouse perspective, seeing their lead in the American League Central shrink to 1.5 games ahead of a crucial six-day road trip that ends with three matchups against the second-place Cleveland Guardians means they’re at risk of upsetting what should be the natural order.</p><p>“We want to win the division because we feel like we are the best team in the division–that’s what should happen,” said infielder Colson Montgomery. “Nobody is going to let us run off and have all this stuff. We have to earn all this and we are all well aware of that. We just sit back and see what we are made of.”</p><p>“Sit back and see,” might be the crucial phrase. The Sox have lost eight of their last 11 entering FRiday, were just swept by the fourth-place Pirates, and are a game under .500 since the end of May. As a club defined by charming dugout buffoonery and–in Montgomery’s words–a “we don’t know what we don’t know” innocence, they would rather harken back to the relaxed approach of their first half than lock into some new mode of hyper-seriousness for a decisive final stretch.</p><p>“We don’t need to do anything more than be what we are,” said Sean Burke, who will start the series opener on Monday in Cleveland. “We cared just as much in May as we do right now. An added ‘Oh we <i>really</i> care about these games’ is kind of counterintuitive for us.”</p><p>Speaking of counterintuitive, Burke’s 156 innings pitched this year are a career-high and two of the worst starts of his young career have come in his last three outings. That’s led to questions about fatigue, but he’s actually re-installed some elements of his routine, like long toss, that he had been cutting out for the sake of “saving bullets.”</p><p>The larger lesson in there is that what got the Sox to this point, should be good enough to bring home an AL Central title. Similarly, they can fret about losing ground the past two weeks, but entering their final five series up two games in the loss column over Cleveland and needing just one head-to-head win to clinch the season series and claim the tiebreaker, is clearly the best spot to be in.</p><p>“We're not hitting the panic button,” said ace reliever Grant Taylor. “The fact that we're coming near the end of the season doesn't change the way we've been playing. We've had success with how we've been playing.”</p><p>That said, as young as Will Venable might look for a manager, part of his appeal is his time with the 2023 Rangers means he can draw from World Series experience. And the feasibility of treating the end of a division race like normal games might be one of those things his young team doesn’t know that they don’t know.</p><p>"You want to keep it as normal, because normal has got us into this position,” Venable said. “But there's just a lot of things working against you to keep things normal. For us it's just acknowledging those things, being aware of them and just also understanding that we're in a great spot.”</p><p>In baseball, part of being in a great spot is that the games at the end mean enough to be anxiety-inducing. The Sox might be about to get a lesson in such matters. But for the moment, they present like they could be immune.</p><p>“If you told fans and everyone we are in the position we are in right now, they would probably be pretty happy,” Montgomery said. “We’ve had a couple of series where it’s been a little shaky. Gotta be patient. We know things are going to pass.”</p>

entries.title: Winning Game 1 will help Bears silence corrosive regression talk
entries.summary: <p>Brimstone doesn’t always come with the fire. Sometimes the fire stands alone. Burning with desire and intensity and intention. A divine destruction.</p><p>Let’s start here. My colleague Jason Lieser <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/09/whats-the-best-case-scenario-for-the-2026-bears-as-they-try-to-top-last-seasons-wild-ride" >wrote earlier this week </a>. . . the everything: “If things go as well as reasonably possible for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a>, they could one-up last season and go 12-5 to take the NFC North for a second consecutive year. The road to that destination would start with a convincing win at the Panthers in the season opener Sunday.”</p><p>Not to overstate or make heavy his words, but the “start with a convincing win” that follows the “road to that destination,” if nothing else, provides the perfect framing for the importance of Game 1 of the official beginning of Phase 2 of this modern-era project called the Bears. And how the game Sunday — while only one game in theory looms much bigger in the overall picture of this season — is far more than just one game.</p><p>Because, see, the word “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/09/bears-worst-case-scenario-2026-season-defense-takeaways-popgun-caleb-williams-nfc-north-ben-johnson" >regression</a>” seems to have attached itself to the Bears as the kickoff approaches. These TV types and microphone fiends, YouTube Channel in Mom’s Basement pundits, the ESPNs, Sports Illustrateds, Bleacher Reports of the world, these self-anointed football “experts” on Substack all seem to have come to the conclusion that this next episode for the Bears will be nothing like the last and the results far less celebratory.</p><p>The “NFL’s top regression team” is their overall prediction market. Opinioning and opining on how the Bears will be this year’s Commanders. That even without the Patrick Mahomes/Chiefs return-to-glory pressure or the absurd Rams undefeated-season expectations (in addition, no Jordan Love or C.J. Stroud or Jayden Daniels “save the entire franchise this season or else” attached to Caleb Williams’ arm and in-game decision-making), the Bears will still feel the burden (no Luther intended) of everything that proves regressing wrong every week they step on the field.</p><p>And this Week 1 for them will be the thesis for the other 16. A win against the Panthers speaks loud, a loss louder. This game goes back to their trade three years ago that changed the trajectory of both franchises. It resulted in both being atop their respective divisions last season and both getting beaten by a field goal by the same team last year in the playoffs (Panthers in the wild-card round, Bears in the divisional round) that this season the entire football world believed was unbeatable.</p><p>They share the common thread of being parts of the reason expectations on their growth this season are so iffy. They share the same predicted regressive gene. Built to exceed, set up to fall. The coach who wins this game can use it for the rest of the season as the barometer of what his team is capable of doing when the schedule puts an on-field, in-game mirror in front of them. The other coach has to “find a way” (remember that phrase) to convince his team — and fan base — that Game 1 was only one game; he has to believe his own lie.</p><p>Between offseason departures and injuries, the Bears unquestionably will be missing Kevin Byard III, Nahshon Wright, DJ Moore, Jaquan Brisker, Tremaine Edmunds, C.J. Gardner-Johnson, Drew Dalman (to surprise retirement), Ozzy Trapilo and Coby Bryant, along with the saga that is and has been Kyler Gordon. Making them a team that represents a team that has been torn and frayed at the fringes but with just enough of the core intact that it can still be sold off the rack at Balmain.</p><p>The declarations, if any, of the nexts. Dillon Thieneman, Zavion Thomas, preseason darling Jordan van den Berg. The foundational improvement, if any, of an offensive line that is as important to the Bears as the “Dark Side” is to the Seahawks in matching their last-season overachievement. The rebuild of an obsessive secondary, the insertion of a new center, the improvement, if any, of their awakening run game.</p><p>This is coach Ben Johnson’s largest flex moment to date. Or at least the one he will use. It all rests on not losing ground, not losing focus or course, not ever losing confidence. This game will be the wreck or reckoning of the brutal truth the Bears must deal with that could make, elevate or begin the decline of the rest of their season.</p><p>Because progress is the true disputant of regress. Success is its evil. And they both have to start somewhere.</p><p>In sports, they always tell you the rule of thumb along with the other four fingers is how one game doesn’t matter. Unless it’s the last one. That’s so Knute Rockne ago. Because as we all know and have recently watched one game be a team’s ascension or downfall, a beginning or an end. “You can’t play Game 1 like it’s Game 17,” they’ll tell you . . . except when Game 1 is the appraiser of Game 17 having any meaning. Adjudicates for you exactly who you are destined to be.</p><p>Everything the Bears seek is on the other side of Sodom and Gomorrah. We know what that life’s like here, we’ve already had, survived and rebuilt from our fire. Literally. Proverbially. Characteristically. Now it’s time to show the NFL what it looks like on the other side by a team that has walked through it.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox starter Luis Castillo feels he's 'very, very close' to righting ship after working on mechanics
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS, Mo. — After he chafed under a piggybacking role near the end of his Mariners tenure, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> touted the benefits of returning <b>Luis Castillo </b>to a regular starter routine upon arrival, but he doesn’t seem to mind that his start on Saturday will come after eight days of rest.</p><p>“This extra time has been very beneficial,” Castillo told the Sun-Times via an interpreter. “We all have been on the same page. They are supporting me and that's important to me too. Because what I want is to perform at the highest level, as I've done before.”</p><p>Sox general manager <b>Chris Getz</b> said the club is working with Castillo to make adjustments in the leg drive of his delivery, and he threw a bullpen on Wednesday focused on that issue. Castillo’s release point has dipped over the course of the year, which correlates with his recent struggles to command his fastball up in the zone; <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/03/white-sox-keeping-luis-castillo-in-rotation-and-munetaka-murakami-high-in-batting-order-amid-struggles-will-venable-astros-road-trip-zach-bove-al-central-division-playoffs" target="_blank" ><u>a necessary element to set up use of the changeup</u></a> the White Sox would like to see more.</p><p>But that’s just one symptom he’s trying to address.</p><p>"What we're trying to do is to fix the whole mechanic, not just any specific area,” Castillo said via interpreter. “Doing it in that way is going to help to get the release point a little bit higher, or to the point that it used to be before.”</p><p>Referencing old video of the 33-year-old’s best work has been at the center of the Sox’ efforts. Castillo has a 7.52 ERA since arriving via trade and is having the worst season of his career, but feels the nature of his struggles are familiar, and fixable.</p><p>“We're very, very close to fixing the whole thing,” Castillo said via interpreter.</p><h3><b>Not worried about infamy</b></h3><h3></h3><p>With 16 games left, <b>Colson Montgomery</b> is at 202 strikeouts, putting him on pace to surpass–by one–<b>Mark Reynolds’ </b>MLB single-season record of 223 whiffs from 2009. If he’s preoccupied with the record, he’s not showing it.</p><p>“That’s the first time I ever heard about some sort of record,” Montgomery said.</p><p>But Montgomery is plenty aware that he strikes out a lot. He’d like to do it less, but swing-and-miss is also part of his power-oriented game.</p><p>“Everyone doesn’t want to strike out, but sometimes you have to accept it because you are not going to change the way you play,” Montgomery said. “Guys who strike out a lot. You see them, what do they also do? They hit a lot of homers and drive a lot of guys in.”</p><p>To his point, 2009 was Reynolds’ best season, as he hit 44 home runs. Also sitting at 44 home runs for the year right now is Phillies slugger <b>Kyle Schwarber</b>, who is ahead of Montgomery with 205 strikeouts on the season.</p><h3><b>Sore spots</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Off to a slow start (.207/.303/.241 in nine games) in September, manager <b>Will Venable</b> noted that <b>Chase Meidroth</b>’s right wrist discomfort “kind of comes and goes.” Meidroth began wearing a brace for the issue last month.</p><p>Time is running out for <b>Joey Bart</b> to return to action from the hand fracture he suffered via hit-by-pitch in his third game with the Sox after being acquired at the trade deadline. Venable said a recent CT scan showed the injury was still healing.</p>

entries.title: Downers Grove North comes back to beat Glenbard West
entries.summary: <p>Downers Grove North's Kevin Jay only played one series last week and it went down to the wire whether he'd play this week.</p><p>But the senior stepped in when needed and delivered the throws that helped the No. 17 Trojans get past No. 15 Glenbard West 24-14 Friday night in Downers Grove.</p><p>Jay threw touchdown passes to Ray Johnson and Grant Georgas, the latter an 11-yarder with 3:12 left in the third quarter to put Downers North up 17-14. Georgas' 59-yard TD run at 3:12 of the fourth quarter all but sealed the win for the Trojans (4-0, 2-0 West Suburban Silver).</p><p>It capped an eventful week for Jay, known more for his running than throwing. But the lingering injury flipped his script.</p><p>"I played the first drive [in a 28-0 win against Hinsdale Central], got kind of twisted up on," Jay said. "Decided it was best for me to sit the rest of that game.</p><p>This week, "I wasn't feeling the best, but I kept [going] through my recovery and what the trainers told me to do. And it got better over the week. So [Thursday] I made the decision that I was ready to play, and I could play 100%."</p><p>But junior Joey Goodwin started at quarterback and was 5-of-8 passing for 49 yards.</p><p>"Joey, our previous quarterback, had a little bit of a hit," Trojans coach Joe Horeni said. "So we wanted to be smart about it with him in terms of injury.</p><p>"KJ [Jay] was hurt last week, so we were going to [go] sparingly with him if we needed to. And then obviously we needed to play him."</p><p>Jay finished 7-of-17 passing for 74 with two interceptions.</p><p>He was on the other side of a similar scenario last year when he started for Downers North in place of current Minnesota freshman Owen Lansu against Glenbard West. The Trojans fell behind 28-0 in the first quarter of that game and lost 35-21.</p><p>"I didn't perform very well [then]," Jay said. "... So it was definitely a chip on my shoulder going into this game."</p><p>It helped having Georgas and Zachary Surowiec to share the load. Georgas ran 22 times for 159 yards and Surowiec had nine carries for 41 yards.</p><p>"I trust in those guys," Jay said. "I know if anything happened to me, we could still run the ball how we should with them."</p><p>Glenbard West (2-2, 1-1) scored on two long runs in the first 13 minutes of the game, a 77-yarder down the left sideline by Keyante Johnson and a 76-yarder down the right sideline by quarterback AJ Rayford. That put the Hilltoppers up 14-3, but they were outscored 21-0 the rest of the way.</p><p>Rayford was 15-of-20 passing for 157 yards with one interception and ran six times for 84 yards. Keyante Johnson had six carries for 100 yards and six catches for 39 yards.</p><p>"I thought we played pretty good defensively," Hilltoppers coach Chad Hetlet said. "... We just didn't execute as good as we possibly could on offense. But give credit to Downers, they've done a really good job.</p><p>"We're super inexperienced and young. We played with a lot of injuries on defense, so we've got a lot of guys who grew up tonight and I'm proud of the way they fought."<br></p>

entries.title: Will Mettee leads Loyola's defense and sparks the offense to a thrilling win against Brother Rice
entries.summary: <p>Loyola linebacker Will Mettee is well-known in the Catholic League Blue, but the Boston College recruit isn’t one of the state’s headline stars.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/09/10/high-school-football-scores-chicago-illinois" >Friday</a> in Wilmette, in the biggest local game of the high school football season so far, up against some of the country’s most highly recruited players, Mettee was the best player on the field. The 6-2, 225-pound linebacker starred on both sides of the ball in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/09/06/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >top-ranked</a> Loyola’s 27-24 win against No. 6 Brother Rice.</p><p>Mettee led the Ramblers’ ferocious defense mentally and emotionally. He contributed a sack and two TFLs and scored two touchdowns, both in completely different ways.</p><p>In the first quarter, Brother Rice quarterback Sam Holcomb had the ball stripped, and Mettee grabbed it before it hit the ground and ran 30 yards for a touchdown.</p><p>Then late in the fourth quarter with Loyola trailing 17-13, Mettee checked in at fullback and powered through Brother Rice’s vaunted defensive line for a crucial two-yard touchdown on third down.</p><p>“That was probably my favorite high school football memory right there,” Mettee said. “Getting the ball on the two-yard line with not a lot of time left to go and making it happen. I’m really proud of myself but mostly proud of my team.”</p><p>Mettee expected to get some playing time at fullback this season. Loyola coach John Holecek wants to save that for the big moments.</p><p>“In the playoffs he will be there,” Holecek said. “It is a long season, especially in the Catholic League. Mettee is a pure football player. He is strong and conditioned. Boston College is getting a heck of a player.”</p><p>Brother Rice (2-2, 0-1 Catholic Blue) responded quickly after Mettee’s touchdown run and took a 24-20 lead with 3:08 left on a 44-yard TD pass from Rocco Galasso to Lucas Strang.</p><p>That left the game in the hands of Matthew Lee and the Ramblers’ offense. Lee started the season strong, but this was his first real high-profile, high-pressure Catholic League Blue moment, and he delivered.</p><p>Lee connected with Joe Haughey on a 46-yard touchdown to put Loyola (4-0, 1-0) ahead for good with 1:10 left.</p><p>“[Lee] was off in the first three quarters,” Holecek said. “I didn’t feel like he was his natural self. entries.title: Bears defense enters opener with more questions than answers
entries.summary: <p>Since the last time they played a meaningful snap, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> have lost more on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/09/bears-worst-case-scenario-2026-season-defense-takeaways-popgun-caleb-williams-nfc-north-ben-johnson" target="_blank" >defense</a> than they’ve gained.</p><p>Safety Kevin Byard, the NFL’s interceptions leader last year, and cornerback Nahshon Wright, its takeaway leader, each left for free agency. The Bears cut Tremaine Edmunds, who was third among all linebackers in interceptions, in a cost-saving move.</p><p>Slot cornerback Kyler Gordon is hurt and will miss at least the next four games because of a calf injury that’s bothered him since the spring. Safety Coby Bryant, the team’s high-priced free-agency addition, is out until at least December with a knee injury. And defensive tackle Gervon Dexter, who was second on the team in sacks last year, got traded last month before he could get cut.</p><p>In their place step speedy linebacker Devin Bush, safety and first-round pick Dillon Thieneman and a rotation of defensive tackles. And, notably, no new edge rushers.</p><p>“You can’t really replace those guys, but we have to try our best to do so,” defensive end Montez Sweat told the Sun-Times on Friday. “The new guys have got to step up and the leaders have to put more on our shoulders.”</p><p>When the Bears take the field for their season opener Sunday at the Panthers, then, there will be more questions than answers. Namely: how, exactly, is the defense better this season?</p><p>“I think it's still to be determined,” coordinator Dennis Allen said.</p><p>He likes the buy-in he got from his players, who spent the spring months focusing more on their fundamentals than playing the calls in his system. The Bears added speed, at Allen’s insistence. Still, the Bears have to break in new starters at defensive tackle, linebacker, cornerback and safety.</p><p>“We’re hard-nosed, we’re going to play physical, we’re going to play fast, we’re going to play poised …” Bush said. “We’re still developing and still learning what that looks like realistically once we get to Week 1 and Week 2 and Week 3.”</p><p>Last year, the Bears actually won games because of a defense that led the NFL in takeaways. That masked problems — they gave up the 10<sup>th</sup>-most points in the NFL, and were the only team in the bottom 10 to make the playoffs. If the Bears want to win more than one postseason game this year, their defense needs to be better.</p><p>Sunday might mark the start of the Bears’ great Faustian bargain. When Bears fans prayed for their team to return to relevance, would they have ever known that it wasn’t because of anything their defense did?</p><p>If they’re going to get any farther than the second round of the playoffs, though, their defense needs to find answers.</p><p>“I have an idea of what it’s supposed to look like,” Sweat said. “Whether we get to it is up to us. We’ll see how we do on Sunday.”</p>

entries.title: Review sentencing of violence survivors who defended themselves
entries.summary: <p>Keshia Golden’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/24/prosecutors-expected-to-offer-new-deal-to-woman-accused-of-killing-boyfriend-as-trial-kicks-off" >plea deal acceptance</a> was a bittersweet victory after courageously fighting a legal system historically stacked against survivors criminalized for defending themselves. Despite more than 50 police calls, four arrests documenting her partner’s abuse and an order of protection, she was eight months pregnant when, fearing for her life and that of her unborn child, she stabbed him in his leg in self-defense and was charged with first-degree murder, facing up to 60 years in prison.</p><p>The reduced charge of involuntary manslaughter and probation is a victory, enabling her to continue caring for her daughter. But even a conviction without incarceration can create lifelong barriers to housing, education, employment and stability, particularly for Black women who are disproportionately criminalized and incarcerated.</p><p>In Cook County, multiple survivors of domestic violence have been charged for fighting back against their abusers. There were at least two cases in the last year where survivors fought murder charges for over a decade only to be found not guilty. These survivors lost housing, jobs, stability for their children and their freedom.</p><p>Across the nation, nearly three women a day are <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/domestic-violence-nearly-three-u-s-women-killed-every-day-n745166" target="_blank" >killed</a> by an intimate partner. In Chicago, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/investigating-injustice-black-women-domestic-violence-victims-chicago/" target="_blank" >3 of every 4</a> domestic battery victims are women. The majority of women in state prisons have histories of domestic violence, sexual assault and other forms of abuse.</p><p>The outcome in Golden’s case forces us to confront these realities. There are hundreds of women in Illinois prisons whose experiences of abuse and survival were never fully considered. State’s attorney’s offices have the power to drop charges in current cases and to agree to resentencing petitions for dozens of survivors under Illinois’ <a class="Link" href="https://the-network.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/MeasuringSafety24_103ILGenAssembly.pdf" target="_blank" >Gender-Based Violence Resentencing Act</a>. These survivors, many who served decades in prison for defending themselves, can and should be released in cooperation with state’s attorneys offices across Illinois.</p><p>The Women’s Justice Institute, along with advocacy organizations that make up the Alliance in Support of Criminalized Survivors, are calling on officials with the Cook County state’s attorney’s office to meet with us to review the cases where survivors are facing criminal charges for choosing to fight back. This approach should be replicated statewide, and we stand ready to help build it.</p><p>The contradictions must end now: We cannot celebrate progress in public safety while criminalizing survivors of domestic violence for refusing to die quietly.</p><p><i>Deanne Benos, executive director, Women’s Justice Institute</i><br><i>Alexis Mansfield, director of policy and special projects, Women’s Justice Institute</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7b0000" name="module-7b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Take postpartum illness seriously </h3><p>When will America recognize how deadly postpartum psychosis is?</p><p>New mothers do not kill their babies or themselves because they are murderers. Their illness causes them to do it.</p><p>My <a class="Link" href="https://www.melaniesbattle.org/story.html" target="_blank" >daughter</a>, Melanie Stokes, jumped from a window after her baby was born. She said her baby hated her because she was a bad mom. The baby was 2 weeks old. She said her husband needed a new wife.</p><p>These new moms are delusional and in another world.</p><p>They do not understand what is or might be wrong because the illness has taken over their mind.</p><p>They should not go to prison. They need help. My heart breaks when I read about these new moms.</p><p><i>Carol Blocker, Bronzeville</i></p><h3>Make polluters pay</h3><p>Many of us are familiar with this viral <a class="Link" href="https://cleanenergy.org/news/from-abstract-to-reality-when-your-hometown-becomes-a-climate-casualty/" target="_blank" >quote</a> we've seen on social media: “Climate change will manifest as a series of disasters viewed through phones with footage that gets closer and closer to where you live until you’re the one filming it."</p><p>This summer, Chicagoans took photos of massive trees falling on cars and homes after violent, unpredictable storms. We scrolled through videos of flooded streets and basements filled with sewage. We watched news about the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/13/5-tornadoes-confirmed-illinois-total-25-tuesday-storms" target="_blank" >record-breaking tornadoes</a>,<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/14/near-record-breaking-heat-expected-as-sizzling-heat-wave-continues" target="_blank" > record-breaking heat</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/07/16/wildfire-smoke-air-quality-illinois/" target="_blank" >record-breaking air quality</a>. And then there were things we couldn't film: sleepless nights in a sweltering apartment, itchy eyes and aching chests from wildfire smoke and worry for loved ones who work outside.</p><p>In 2024, climate and extreme weather events cost Illinois nearly <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2025/01/20/illinois-affected-by-a-record-number-of-billion-dollar-climate-disasters-in-2024-mostly-severe-storms/" target="_blank" >$4 billion</a> in damages. Chicagoans pay with our money, health and lives, but data shows we aren’t the ones responsible. <a class="Link" href="https://climateaccountability.org/carbon-majors/" target="_blank" >Reports</a> trace 71% of global industrial emissions to 100 fossil fuel producers. These companies understand the devastation they cause. By 1977, Exxon’s own cutting-edge climate <a class="Link" href="https://insideclimatenews.org/project/exxon-the-road-not-taken/" target="_blank" >research</a> predicted global temperatures would increase by 2 to 3 degrees Celsius. Yet Exxon chose to deny its own findings, discredit future climate science and lobby against the climate action we needed, all while the industry accrued nearly <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/jul/21/revealed-oil-sectors-staggering-profits-last-50-years" target="_blank" ><u>$1 trillion</u></a> in profits annually over the last 50 years. Exxon knew, and still decided the profits were worth more than the floods, heat, smoke and all the families who would suffer from a mess they didn’t make.</p><p>It’s time to balance the scale. Following the lead of Vermont and New York, the proposed <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus/FullText?GAID=18&DocNum=2981&DocTypeID=SB&LegId=165475&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >Illinois Climate Change Superfund Act </a>— House Bill 4773 and Senate Bill 2981— applies a similar legal framework as the 1980 federal Superfund laws, which forced chemical companies to clean up toxic spills. This act requires oil and gas companies to pay for climate adaptation, providing Illinois with billions for vital projects like flood control and cooling centers. Disadvantaged communities, which often face the worst environmental injustices, would receive 40% of funding.</p><p>We no longer need to look at climate change through our phones. Just look up. It’s here, and we need resources to adapt. Join the Make Polluters Pay Coalition and call your elected leaders and demand they co-sponsor the Climate Change Superfund Act to ensure those responsible for this mess pay. </p><p><i>Aleah Rogalski, </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.onenorthside.org/" target="_blank" ><i>ONE Northside</i></a><i> volunteer,</i> <i>Lake View</i></p><h3>Students need help curbing absenteeism </h3><p>As we work to address chronic absenteeism in Chicago Public Schools, we need to acknowledge that the conversation and effort is falling short. Venture philanthropy is not the solution, and in fact, could be adding to the issue by focusing solely on the "return on investment" and treating real people as numbers on a dashboard.</p><p>Chronic absenteeism leads to several negative outcomes, ranging from <a class="Link" href="https://dpi.illinois.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Absenteeism_Report_final.pdf" target="_blank" >decreased student disengagement to increased dropout rates</a>. While providing additional mental health and family support may seem like the solution, all it does is continue to place the blame on individuals for their circumstances instead of addressing the systemic racism and poverty that have created these inequities.</p><p>At CPS, 71.8% students are economically disadvantaged, 17.3% have disabilities, and 88% are people of color. Students with disabilities are <a class="Link" href="https://www.ed.gov/teaching-and-administration/supporting-students/chronic-absenteeism" target="_blank" >three times more likely to be chronically absent</a>, with <a class="Link" href="https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1393027" target="_blank" ><u>asthma as the leading cause of health-related school absences</u></a>. Couple these issues with other systemic barriers, such as living in a transportation and medical desert, and now you have a parent taking all day to get to get his or her child to a needed medical appointment instead of school. These scenarios make it clear we need to start <a class="Link" href="http://chronic-absence-report_final-2.pdf/" target="_blank" >framing chronic absenteeism as a public health issue</a>.</p><p>Even when youth overcome barriers to get to school, they're often faced with <a class="Link" href="https://stand.org/illinois/our-stories/exploring-chronic-absenteeism-illinois/" target="_blank" >punitive practices, bullying and a lack of positive relationships</a>. At a time where chronic absenteeism is soaring at about 40%, we continue to disinvest in school practices that build culture, like restorative justice and trauma-informed support, while prioritizing band-aid interventions instead.</p><p>We need real solutions in our communities. Research has shown that school-based health centers that offer on-site care <a class="Link" href="https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2025/05/attendance-improves-rural-nys-schools-site-health-clinics" target="_blank" >can reduce a young person’s risk of chronic absenteeism by as much as 15%</a>. If a health center can make that much of a difference, imagine a community hub model that includes food pantries, eviction defense, housing services, mental health counseling and transportation for the whole family?</p><p>To move the needle on the issue of chronic absenteeism, we need to show our communities that we value them as whole people by funding comprehensive solutions to root causes.</p><p><i>Bessie Alcantara, executive director, </i><a class="Link" href="http://alternativesyouth.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Alternatives</i></a></p><h3>Safeguard current workforce under rural health plan </h3><p>Illinois has a rare opportunity to strengthen rural healthcare with <a class="Link" href="https://hfs.illinois.gov/info/fedresctr/ruralhealthtp.html" target="_blank" >$193.4 million</a> in first-year funding through the federal Rural Health Transformation Program.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://icahn.org/" target="_blank" >Illinois Critical Access Hospital Network</a> <a class="Link" href="https://icahn.org/news/news-release-icahn-awarded-more-than-50-million-by-the-state-of-illinois-to-advance-rural-healthcare-transformation-across-illinois/" target="_blank" >announced</a> last month it will administer $5 million for hospital workforce investment and long-term workforce sustainability — illustrating a real understanding that healthcare professionals need support today and a plan for the future. While training is hugely important, healthcare facilities also need to consider how to fill a shift for this weekend.</p><p>We learned in prior crises that there are many health licensed professionals willing to work, but they require schedule flexibility to reenter the profession.</p><p>An August survey of 150 Illinois nurses, certified nursing assistants and direct care workers who use ShiftKey, a digital platform connecting independent healthcare professionals with open facility shifts, found that 96% said schedule choice was very important to their decision to remain in healthcare. Even more striking, 91% said they would work fewer hours or leave the field entirely if flexible, independent contractor shift options were no longer available.</p><p>Independent work is not a substitute for a strong full-time workforce. For parents, caregivers, students and others who cannot commit to a traditional schedule, it’s what keeps them in the workforce.</p><p>Independent work also helps facilities respond to immediate needs. In the same ShiftKey survey, 95% of respondents said flexible shift work allowed them to pick up shifts at short-staffed Illinois facilities in the past year that they otherwise would not have worked.</p><p>Illinois understands the needs of today and tomorrow and can build the healthcare workforce of tomorrow and provide opportunities for health professionals that for this moment in their lives need flexibility to work today. Investments in nursing education, recruitment and retention should go hand in hand with policies that preserve multiple ways for licensed professionals to participate in the workforce.</p><p>The goal of the Rural Health Transformation Program should bring together additional licensed professionals along with additional schedule flexibilities — not force every clinician into a singular employment model that doesn't<b> </b>meet the needs of all licensed professionals.</p><p>This will ensure a pipeline today and tomorrow of qualified professionals capable and ready to care for Illinois patients — especially in communities where every available worker counts.</p><p><i>Dr. Deborah L. Birx, former White House coronavirus response coordinator and U.S. Global AIDS coordinator</i></p><h3>Bearing traffic</h3><p>I drive the Interstate 94 and Interstate 80 corridor frequently. The traffic at the state line is often congested and goes in both directions from morning until past sunset seven days a week.</p><p>Imagine an additional 25,000 vehicles trying to get to a Bears game? Lake Forrest personnel better have early lunches and leave, or they may miss the first half. What about Monday or Thursday night games?</p><p><i>Gregory Collins, Antioch</i></p><h3>Religious term doesn’t belong in football </h3><p>In the sports section of Monday's Sun-Times, a subheadline of a USA Today story read "Big Ten officials gave the Wolverines time to pull off Hail Mary."</p><p>However, the article wasn't about the University of Michigan football team players huddling up to say a prayer that Roman Catholics recite to honor a person they believe to be the mother of God.</p><p>Instead, the article detailed how the Michigan team was given time to attempt a last-second, game-winning pass play that only had a "prayer" of a chance of being successful.</p><p>I believe it is well past time that the football world and media discontinue using this phrase in a manner that Catholics such as myself feel can only diminish the sanctity of the actual prayer.</p><p><i>Patrick J. Molony, Alsip</i></p><h3>Football isn’t only dangerous sport</h3><p>With all of the justifiable emphasis on concussion protocol and chronic traumatic encephalopathy in the NFL, why don’t we see stories of professional boxers or UFC fighters having concussion protocol or CTE? It seems with athletes punching each other in the head over and over it could be more of a problem than in the NFL.</p><p><i>Jim Hogan, Palos Hills</i></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Gift of signed baseball bat came with strings attached
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> About 15 years ago, my nephew gave me a birthday gift of a baseball bat signed by a top player. I love baseball, so it was a lovely gift. After I thanked him, he said, "When my son is older, I would like you to give it to him." We have been estranged now for at least 10 years because his spouse dislikes our family for some reason.</p><p>Am I obligated to find a way to get the bat back to him? Looking at their Facebook over the years, I see no signs that there is any interest in baseball in this son or their family. I am in my later years and have been trying to downsize and pass on some of my things. I would rather pass it on to a grandchild of mine who loves and currently plays baseball and would treasure it. — <i>DOWNSIZING BASEBALL FAN</i></p><p><b>DEAR FAN:</b> This family has chosen to cut ties with you. They cannot reasonably expect you to track down a grandnephew with whom you have no relationship. In fact, it was crass of your nephew to put a stipulation on the gift in the first place. Pass the bat to the grandchild you know and love.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I've been married for 20 years. My in-laws and I have had a decent relationship. My husband, our three teenage children and I have been living with them for 10 years. It was rough at first, but things got better.</p><p>My in-laws received and spent three cushy inheritances (close to $3.5 million) over the last 22 years. They also maxed out a reverse mortgage within the past two years. Abby, they have not one dime of it left!</p><p>Things started to go downhill about four years ago. My husband and I have bailed them out financially too many times to count. We're not financially struggling, but our nest egg (that we worked hard for and was to go toward buying our own home) is nearly gone. The in-laws have slid back into their old ways again — not paying bills, not cleaning up after themselves, not helping with household chores, neglecting their health, etc.</p><p>My in-laws gave us their powers of attorney for health and finance a few months ago. They agreed to allow us to help them get organized, make a budget, clean up their house, make appointments and hold them accountable. They invariably play the victim and complain when we try to discuss things. Over the past eight months, I've had two breakdowns. This is affecting my mental and physical health. My kids want nothing to do with their grandparents. I'm not perfect, but I do have self-respect. Please help! — <i>ON EDGE IN WASHINGTON</i></p><p><b>DEAR ON EDGE:</b> It's time to recognize that your in-laws may have a problem that you and your husband are not equipped to handle. That you now have their powers of attorney may (or may not) save all of you. For everyone's sake, stop enabling them and enlist the help of a licensed financial counselor to help straighten out this mess. Go online and look for an accredited or certified credit counselor affiliated with the National Foundation for Credit Counseling (nfcc.org.). Their "slide back into their old ways" may have a medical explanation, which means your in-laws need to be evaluated medically and neurologically. Please don't wait.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Here's how some Chicago small businesses are ramping up their use of AI
entries.summary: <p>During the COVID-19 pandemic, Chris Clark was furloughed from his corporate job. So he started giving tennis lessons in Lincoln Park’s Oz Park.</p><p>The former college tennis player has built his onetime side hustle into the racket sports company Toss and Spin, which has offered more than 8,000 classes.</p><p>Clark says he was overwhelmed at first by needing to deal with 50 to 100 inquiries a day from customers.So he searched for a system to handle customer service and email and SMS marketing.</p><p>He evaluated 15 different platforms and chose Chicago's ActiveCampaign, which uses AI to automate responses to customers. He says its real-time AI analytics also offered quicker customer insights and replaced months of manual research for Toss and Spin. ActiveCampaign tailored promotions to Toss and Spin’s customers and helped launch specialized sports programs that sold out. And automated texts converted first-time customers into repeat clients.</p><p>Like Toss and Spin, many small business owners have turned to AI, though many are still trying to understand how to apply it and are in the early stages of adoption, according to a report by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Yet the AI momentum for small business appears to be growing as business owners look for ways to hold down costs in the face of inflation and labor shortages.</p><p>Nationwide, AI usage has ramped up sharply. In the United States, 87% of small- and medium-sized businesses in a survey are using AI in marketing, according to an analysis released in June by online marketing firm Constant Contact. That’s a big jump from the 26% that reported using AI in 2023.</p><p>Founded in 2003, ActiveCampaign is a $3 billion AI marketing platform used by small businesses worldwide, according to the company, whose offices are in the Loop. In February, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/02/04/chicago-software-firm-activecampaign-buys-ai-startup-feedback-intelligence" target="_blank" >ActiveCampaign</a> bought the AI startup Feedback Intelligence in San Francisco and helped ramp up its AI capabilities.</p><p>In August, ActiveCampaign launched an AI service called Wavelength that it says continuously analyzes a client’s account, including sent messages and who’s engaged. “The more it runs, the sharper it gets,” according to the company, which says it reflects “customers’ evolving behavior rather than a playbook scraped from everyone else.”</p><p>“The era of prompt and response is over,” says Jason VandeBoom, ActiveCampaign's chief executive officer. The company’s AI-driven marketing “means a model that can look at how past campaigns have performed, ideate a new campaign unique to the user’s offering and their target audiences, then execute on it, if approved by the user.”</p><p>Many small businesses are using AI for routine tasks such as drafting emails and marketing content, summarizing documents and managing schedules, according to the U.S. Chamber. Businesses are using AI scheduling assistants to reduce missed appointments and increase weekly service calls. Companies are also using AI for billing, invoicing, inventory tracking and basic customer service.</p><p>“Many of our customers are very small marketing teams that need a tool that can ideate and produce the work of a much larger team,” VandeBoom says.</p><h3>Saving time</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2025/07/01/social-venture-mona-microlender-kiva-loans-chicago-entrepreneurs" >Mona</a>, a tech platform that connects small businesses to loans and grants, works with thousands of small businesses across the United States. Many have adopted AI tools, according to Mona co-founder Andrew Leon Hanna.</p><p>“In general, the small businesses that are most successful with AI are not using it just for the sake of using AI but toward a clear business goal — tied directly to increasing revenue or decreasing costs, including saving time, as that is small business owners’ greatest asset,” says Hanna, who is also an adjunct professor at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business.</p><p>Hanna says common AI tasks among small businesses include using OpenAI’s Codex to pre-draft emails, using AI voice agents to summarize meetings and draft invoices or proposals while driving or in transit and building AI agents to respond to customer reviews on Yelp.</p><p>Chicago accessory maker Ecodunia noticed a low conversion rate of browsers to buyers on its e-commerce site, Hanna says.</p><p>Ecodunia founder Cera Muchiri revamped the website’s product photos using AI photo editing tools like Nano Banana, which led to increased sales.</p><p>Half of Constant Contact’s survey respondents said saving time is the top benefit of using AI, with 42% using it to write emails and social media posts. Forty percent are investing in AI usage rather than advertising and 38% are using it to analyze data.</p><p>Contractors are testing AI on more complex tasks such as flagging scheduling risks and estimating project costs, according to the U.S. Chamber, which says manufacturers are using it to predict equipment maintenance issues before they cause breakdowns.</p><p>The ways small businesses are using AI range widely, with some testing it out to tech companies that are investing heavily in it. But many lack the training to scale up AI. Concerns around cost, unclear return on investment and compliance risks are also barriers, according to the national business group.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Roger Simon, beloved Sun-Times political columnist, dies at 78
entries.summary: <p>Columnist Roger Simon, who for 40 years covered every presidential election, joked about his need to be buried in his hometown of Chicago, despite living in Washington, D.C. for half his life. </p><p>That way, he would say, he could still vote in Chicago elections since dead people can vote<b>.</b></p><p>Simon was a beloved columnist for a number of publications, including the Chicago Sun-Times and Politico, where he was the chief political columnist. He was known for writing about the dramatics of politics with engaging humor and wit, making complex topics understandable for readers.</p><p>On Thursday, after a short bout of pneumonia, Simon died in Washington D.C., at 78.</p><p>His wife of nearly 50 years, fellow journalist and longtime copy editor at the Washington Post Marcia Kramer Simon, said he wanted to be buried in Chicago because he was “Chicago to his core.”</p><p>“He loved Chicago and Chicago loved him back,” Kramer Simon, 77, told the Sun-Times. </p><p>Roger Simon was born in Chicago on March 29, 1948. His father was a truck driver, and his mother was a homemaker.</p><p>Simon cobbled together student loans and scholarships to attend the University of Illinois, where he pursued a love of journalism at the student newspaper.</p><p>That’s where he met his future wife, Marcia, as a sophomore. At the time, he was dating someone he'd known from high school, but when they broke up, his friendship with Marcia blossomed into something more. </p><p>Their first date was on her 19th birthday, she said.</p><p>They would be together for the next 58 years.</p><p>The couple later worked together at the Sun-Times. Simon was an investigative reporter for several years before becoming a columnist in 1975. He dove headfirst into thorny political issues, like spousal abuse and racism, and made powerful figures, like then-Gov. James Thompson, his targets.</p><p>He traveled the world reporting, including covering apartheid in South Africa.</p><p>Simon’s work made a visible impact and changed lives in Chicago. His coverage of spousal abuse led the Chicago Police Department to change its classification of such incidents from domestic disturbances to abuse. </p><p>“He changed lives with what he wrote,” Kramer Simon said. “...He had a way with words that people couldn’t touch.”</p><p>After being assigned to cover the 1976 presidential election for the Sun-Times, Simon would maintain that assignment for the next 40 years.</p><p>He wrote popular books on presidential campaigns, most recently on the 2012 presidential race, published in 2013, entitled "Reckoning: Campaign 2012 and the Battle for the Soul of America<i>."</i></p><p>He stayed with the Sun-Times, writing columns until his departure in 1984 after Rupert Murdoch bought the paper. Many columns at the Sun-Times were soon after published in the book, ‘Simon Says: The Best of Roger Simon.”</p><p>Simon and his wife then moved to D.C., where he lived the rest of his life. He continued writing for the Baltimore Banner as a columnist and at Politico.</p><p>But Kramer Simon said he always loved being a columnist at the Sun-Times, a paper he called a “scrappy underdog.”</p><p>“Writing for the Sun-Times, he always said that was the best job he ever had,” she recalled.</p><p>Simon won more than a dozen first-place awards for writing and reporting, and twice won the American Society of Newspaper Editors Distinguished Writing Award for Commentary.</p><p>For over 25 years, his columns were syndicated by Creators Syndicate, where he landed in the homes of thousands of newspaper readers around the world.</p><p>In his final Politico column from 2017, announcing his retirement, he wrote, “I have also been flooded — really, you can read them — with messages on Facebook and Twitter asking me not to retire. Not now. Not, I’m told, when America 'needs' me.</p><p>I know, I know. It is preposterous. It is laughable. But not to some. For some, I have been the friend they have never met for more than 40 years.”</p><p>Simon wrote that he wanted to travel the world with his wife following retirement. But for years, he struggled with his health, eventually contracting sepsis that led to a double leg amputation in 2009</p><p>But he didn’t like to focus on his health problems.</p><p>After announcing his retirement, Simon returned to the Sun-Times as a weekly columnist. He continued writing on politics and the Donald Trump presidency until 2018.</p><p>He loved reading mysteries and science fiction, and had a “modest collection” of art, his wife said. Simon enjoyed traveling before his illnesses and was a Beatles fan. He enjoyed watching television shows like “This Old House,” picking up knowledge — in theory — along the way.</p><p>“He worked with his mind, not his hands,” Kramer Simon said.</p><p>Life with Simon, she said, was stable and steady. He was kind and thoughtful.</p><p>She remembers being drawn to Simon as a friend, and eventual partner, nearly 60 years ago by his sense of humor.</p><p>“I thought he was hilarious with tremendous wit,” she said. “I miss him terribly.”</p><p></p><p></p><p>Simon’s wish to return to Chicago will be fulfilled with a private burial. He is survived by his wife of 49 years and his sister, Lynne Copp (Al Wayne).</p>

entries.title: Review: “The Birth of the Pill” at TimeLine Theatre
entries.summary: <p>Chicago author Jonathan Eig’s non-fiction book, “The Birth of the Pill,” does not come across as an obvious candidate for theatrical adaptation.</p><p>It’s filled with compelling details about the development of the revolutionary contraceptive and spreads its focus out over four characters who are importantly, but not always directly, involved in how the birth control pill came to be. The book lurches forward in fits and starts, as scientific progress often does. It allows the known significance of the social change the pill will bring — enabling sex without fear of pregnancy and all that means — to drive the tale more than suspenseful narrative or personal stakes.</p><p>So there’s no question that its adapter needed a willingness to take theatrical risks. Playwright Jessica Huang certainly brings that.</p><p>Her play of the same name, receiving its world premiere at TimeLine Theatre’s new building in Uptown, brims with creative ideas about how to tell the story. It has a strong point of view that embraces complexity, and finds some inspired moments of humor.</p><p>But clever ideas and an inquisitive perspective can’t always make a play spring to theatrical life, and this one falls squarely into the “noble effort” category. In all honesty, it comes across as a piece still early in development and in need of a fresh conceptual start.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="2.5" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> “The Birth of the Pill” </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-680000" name="module-680000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When</b>: through Oct. 4<br><b>Where</b>: TimeLine Theatre (5035 N. Broadway)<br><b>Tickets</b>: $65-$100<br><b>Info</b>: <a class="Link" href="http://timelinetheatre.com" target="_blank" ><u>timelinetheatre.com</u></a><br><b>Run time</b>: 1 hour and 35 minutes with no intermission</div> </div><p>From the beginning of the play, Huang introduces a new character, narrator Ramona Delgado (María Victoria Martínez), who claims to be a “footnote” in the story. We’ll eventually discover that she is one of the dozens of Puerto Rican women who participated — many without informed consent — in the clinical trials for the pill. Many experienced problematic and even severe side effects; the dosage was much higher than it should have been. In history books, including Eig’s, their stories are treated as little more than a statistic on the road to progress.</p><p>The concept is intriguing and certainly fair. The trials were held in Puerto Rico in part because, unlike in much of the mainland U.S., contraception was legal there. But the attitudes of the main characters – especially Margaret Sanger (Janet Ulrich Brooks), pioneering founder of Planned Parenthood and the driving force behind the pill’s existence – unquestionably included a superiority complex, flirting with eugenics. Yes, the pill would bring women around the world access to reproductive freedom, but she didn’t mind saying it also meant the “wrong” women wouldn’t have so many babies.</p><p>But Ramona’s story remains a vague one. She seems to be an aggregate character, and she comes off as exactly that: a representation, an idea, and in Martínez’s hands, a big personality, but not a person.</p><p>As Ramona, Martínez steps in to play the supporting characters, and Huang also invests her with theatrical powers: The ability to snap her fingers and stop the action. The playwright toys with this, giving that power to Sanger as well. In an early scene, the two battle over who has control of the storytelling. Again, it’s a smart and meaningful idea, but it’s mostly abandoned thereafter, which is welcome because it quickly grinds any forward movement to a halt.</p><p>Still, the scene is entertaining, as are many of the scenes here. Huang and director Sandra Marquez do a particularly fine job with the lab scenes, as researcher Min Chue Chang (a sincere and likable Rammel Chan) explains some of the science and euthanizes (stuffed) rabbits as part of the experiments.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d40000" Fain), the brilliant scientist who had fallen from an academic perch at Harvard for talking too publicly about his work on early in vitro fertilization. But he’s mostly a supporting figure here. The most lively scenes largely belong to Sanger and the wealthy philanthropist Katharine McCormick (Mary Beth Fisher). Ulrich portrays Sanger with an upright posture that signals how intimidating she can be, which makes her an ideal match for Fisher’s comic yet convincing take on fur-wearing McCormick, overflowing with a carefree nonchalance only massive wealth can provide.</p><p>Huang and actor David Parkes also have a lot of fun with the character of John Rock, the trusted, earnest, Catholic gynecologist who here serves as an emblem of walking testosterone.</p><p>These excellent performances suggest there would be other promising ways into this story, as we can see the very different yet essential qualities they each brought to the project’s success.</p><p>By centering the play around Ramona, and yet never really letting her enter the story, Huang unfortunately creates argument but not drama. The play starts fading early, and the final scene — in which Eig himself appears (portrayed by Fain, again) — falls flat.</p><p>It sums up the problem here: This version of “The Birth of the Pill” doesn’t feel so much like storytelling as commentary.</p>

class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cannabis/2019/12/31/21043878/legal-weed-marijuana-emergency-room-visits" target="_blank" ><u>predicted</u></a> an increase in emergency room visits due to consumption of products with higher THC concentrations.</p><p>Those predictions have come to pass, according to Dr. Maria Rahmandar, an event panelist and medical director of the substance use and prevention program at Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago.</p><p>“There is a risk of cannabis-induced psychosis following cannabis use, particularly in young people,” she said, explaining teen consumption of highly concentrated products.</p><p>In 2023, five teens were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/4/19/23690355/5-teens-hospitalized-after-taking-edibles-at-uptown-high-school" target="_blank" ><u>hospitalized</u></a> after taking gummies while at school at an Uptown neighborhood high school.</p><p>In Illinois, people are most likely to start using cannabis between the ages of 18 and 25, according to the Illinois Cannabis Project at the University of Illinois Chicago. But youths ages 12-17 are not far behind.</p><p>Kenwood Academy Principal Karen Calloway said she hopes this is the first of many events to address the community's fears.</p><p>“I think it's important because we have a large population of Chicago public school students,” Calloway said. “We're currently around 2,300 students, and so if we can provide more information to them, I think eventually it becomes a movement around making different and better decisions as it relates to this type of THC usage.”</p><h3><b>Impacts of teen cannabis use</b></h3><p>In 2024, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/12/increasing-medical-marijuana-and-cannabidiol-research/" target="_blank" ><u>U.S. Department of Justice</u></a> issued a proposed rule to reclassify marijuana as a Schedule III drug, which would define it as a drug with less potential harm than Schedule I drugs that are more likely to be abused. This year, Attorney General Todd Blanche <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/04/23/trump-reclassifies-state-licensed-medical-marijuana-as-a-less-dangerous-drug-in-a-historic-shift" target="_blank" ><u>signed an order</u></a> solidifying that reclassification.</p><p>Proponents hailed the move, arguing the drug has medical benefits and that the decision both legitimizes medical marijuana programs and eases barriers to research.</p><p>But critics worry it sends the wrong message to users — especially those who are younger — causing them to underestimate the drug’s effects.</p><p>Johnny’s Ambassadors founder Laura Stack created the nonprofit to educate parents and teens about the dangers of teen cannabis use in honor of her son, who died by suicide after suffering from cannabis-induced psychosis.</p><p>“There's a lot of confusion out there and a lot of misinformation, and we just really want people to understand why teens should not smoke weed,” Stack said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div attend.</p><p>Kimberly McGee, a Chicago police officer, said she’s seen young people overdose on marijuana because it’s been laced with meth or rat poison. She has also seen how it affects young people’s ambition.</p><p>“They have no drive, no motivation,” she said. “It's 'wake up, get dressed, go get high.’ Over and over. They have nothing to look forward to. They don't care.”</p><p>Rahmandar points to advertisements and social media that expose young people to cannabis early on, which encourages them to try it.</p><p>“Regulations that allow for colorful packaging that is marketed to youth without sufficient age verification practices, with Instagram models that are appealing to youth, all of that is very concerning,” Rahmandar said. “[These processes Adderall off the street and take it. You'll smoke whatever they give you out the dispensary.”</p><p>Fellow Grammy-winning songwriter Adam “Bruza” Wright shared his story of smoking four to five joints a day. Now celebrating two years of sobriety, he said he used to smoke because the products he used were a status symbol.</p><p>“It's all just kind of filtering back into consumerism,” Wright said. “And just exploitation because it all just surrounds flex culture, which all comes back to just making you more fanatic and more addictive.”</p><p>Smith said there needs to be a new narrative.</p><p>“But you gotta make it enticing for young people to say, 'I ain't doing that,'" Smith said. “Young people don't really smoke cigarettes. How do we do that?"</p>

entries.summary: <p>This weekend, tourists at Cloud Gate may find themselves drawn to the adjacent Jay Pritzker Pavilion, enticed by music booming from the lawn speakers.</p><p>But when they approach, they’ll find the Millennium Park stage perplexingly empty.</p><p>Without realizing it, they’ve stumbled into <a class="Link" href="https://ess.org/sonic-pavilion/" target="_blank" ><u>Sonic Pavilion</u></a>. The brainchild of local sound-art booster <a class="Link" href="http://ess.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Experimental Sound Studio</u></a>, the festival fashions the Millennium Park lawn into a stage all its own, immersing passersby in sound installations bespoke to its criss-crossing, 24-channel audio system.</p><p>Experimental Sound Studio co-directors Adam Vida, Olivia Junell and Alex Inglizian delight in these accidental encounters. Talk about “sound art,” and the mind may drift to contemporary art museums, galleries and other rarefied settings. But for years, the group has brought the medium to free public spaces, from Millennium Park to the Lincoln Park Conservatory.</p><p>“I still keep in touch with people that have previously been </div></div><p>The group’s support of the city’s sonic arts is similarly multichanneled. Besides these public installations, it hosts a prodigious sound archive that would be the envy of any university, including rare tapes of the Afrofuturist icon Sun Ra and various Chicago free jazz icons. It organizes site-specific live performances, such as a forthcoming, sold-out show at Wisconsin’s Yerkes Observatory featuring trumpeter Rob Mazurek’s Exploding Star Orchestra. It also offers myriad <a class="Link" href="https://ess.org/artist-support/residencies/" target="_blank" ><u>artist residencies</u></a> for creatives looking to develop new work.</p><p>But, as the organization turns 40 this year, Experimental Sound Studio’s behind-the-scenes artist support has plainly become its most essential function. The group helped drive <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/2024/09/27/musician-retirement-fund-chicago-dcase-golden-egg" target="_blank" ><u>Golden Egg</u></a>, an initiative which distributed $50,000 to musician retirement funds last year. (The program is on hiatus while it seeks funding for a second cycle.)</p><p>This year, ESS is piloting a <a class="Link" href="https://ess.org/oes/" target="_blank" ><u>new program</u></a> providing free and discounted studio time at its Edgewater HQ to Chicago-based artists.</p><p>Those projects go a long way. Sifting through 253 applications to Golden Egg last year, Junell and her colleagues learned just how little musicians were actually making: The average reported salary was just under Its first foray was “Train Time,” a 2008 collaboration between Mallozzi and three other composers that collaged train sounds from around the world. Kenthaney Redmond, a flutist, represents the city’s western fringe, in Austin. Trumpeter Mario Abney, a bridge between Chicago and New Orleans’ jazz scenes, represents Washington Park. And <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/morning-shift/2013/08/23/matt-ulery-live-on-morning-shift" target="_blank" ><u>Matt Ulery</u></a>, most known as a bassist but increasingly dusting off his tuba chops, holds down the far northwest side in Norwood Park.</p><p>Each interpreted the same short melody following Black and Diamond’s directions. They were also asked to submit an additional field recording that, to them, summed up what their neighborhood sounds like. Those recordings are woven through the last two minutes of the piece so that it ends with the sounds of the city alone.</p><p>“We feel it's impossible for any one person to be a representative of their neighborhood,” Diamond says. “But we find that living in a specific environment will undoubtedly have some kind of impact, whether conscious or not, on an artist's process.”</p><p>The unique qualities of the Millennium Park sound system also drew in sound artist Kikù Hibino and Cornelius Ferguson, best known to footwork enthusiasts as the revered Corky “Traxman” Strong. Through an audio-processing program, Hibino remixed their collaborative studio session at ESS and spatialized it, sending each of the 24 sound layers ricocheting around the lawn.</p><p>The end result, he says, will sound like a “kaleidoscopic” canopy of fast-paced footwork rhythms and vocal samples. The artists have been so pleased with the project that they’re expanding it into an album, due out this December.</p><p>“I wanted something really pushing the envelope,” Hibino says, “and I know Traxman likes to push the envelope.”</p><p>After Sonic Pavilion wraps, ESS’s 40th anniversary celebrations continue with a <a class="Link" href="https://ess.org/event/40th-celebration/" target="_blank" ><u>free, daylong celebration</u></a> at its Edgewater digs on Oct. 17. And if you miss the festival itself, never fear. Scheduled for December, ESS’s “Sonic Pavilion Redux” has become a tradition-within-a-tradition, adapting the festival commissions for its front gallery’s eight-channel system — no sunscreen required.</p>

entries.title: Legislative inspector general's resignation exposes need for reform
entries.summary: <p>You may know that embattled Legislative Inspector General Michael McCuskey has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/09/08/mike-mccuskey-resigns-benton-report-investigation-complaint" target="_blank" >agreed to resign</a> his post by the end of September.</p><p>But this sorry saga shouldn’t end there. The Legislative Ethics Commission should immediately launch an investigation into why so many women over the years have said they were mistreated, belittled and dismissed by McCuskey.</p><p>They could also ask McCuskey's replacement to revisit the cases.</p><p>And that sounds like what the commission might do. According to state Rep. Jeff Keicher, chair of the Legislative Ethics Commission, “The recent investigations and situations that the LEC has been involved in and the LIG has conducted have revealed points of frustration and pain that the LEC is very interested in closing the gap.”</p><p>Keicher, R-Sycamore, was referring to the inspector general’s investigations into former state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield, and current state Rep. Amy “Murri” Briel, D-Ottawa.</p><p>Benton was found to have sexually harassed women, but a female lobbyist complained that she was mistreated by McCuskey during her interview process.</p><p>Briel was accused of sexually harassing a 2024 campaign worker who eventually moved to her House district office staff.</p><p>Briel has repeatedly claimed that McCuskey ruled the allegations “unfounded,” meaning the claims were made without merit.</p><p>However, McCuskey declared he had made “no finding,” which has no bearing on whether the allegations against Briel were accurate. </p><p>Most of the allegations were about alleged victim Laura Jackson’s campaign work experience, and the legislative inspector general has no authority to look into those. He also ruled that Jackson was an “at will” employee and had no jurisdiction in the matter.</p><p>Either way, Jackson said she experienced many of the same problems as the unnamed female lobbyist reported about McCuskey.</p><p>McCuskey’s alleged behavior wasn’t a “systems” issue. It had little to do with state statutes and rules governing his office.</p><p>Yet, nobody can tell you with a straight face that the law creating the legislative inspector general is adequate. For instance, this one-person quasi-legal tribunal approach to deciding whether sexual harassment allegations are valid doesn’t work on its face, no matter who might be in charge.</p><p>The first thing that has to be done is to make sure those claiming sexual harassment or mistreatment are protected from further harm. Perhaps an ombudsperson could be brought in to help the accusers navigate their paths and maybe even attend interrogations with them (and that interrogation process ought to end as well, of course).</p><p>The office of the legislative inspector general is prohibited from investigating any reports it receives if they are filed more than a year after the alleged wrongdoing. That’s pretty ridiculous. As Rep. Mary Beth Canty, D-Arlington Heights, pointed out in a recent WGN TV interview, House terms are two years, so the limit should be at least that amount of time. </p><p>However, senators serve two four-year terms every 10 years, so there could be room for further expansion.</p><p>The legislative inspector general is also prohibited from investigating stories he or she may have seen in news media reports, unless and until someone files a complaint. That has to be changed.</p><p>Chicago's City Council inspector general's office has some limited enforcement authority over conduct in city campaigns (using images and video taken at places like city fire stations appears to be a favorite campaign thing). Campaign sexual harassment by a legislator or a candidate should be included in the legislative inspector general's portfolio.</p><p>Finally, recent legislative inspector generals have had judicial backgrounds. Those folks are accustomed to lawyers bringing facts and arguments to their courtrooms. The next person in the post should have some investigatory skills to get to the bottom of things, rather than just looking witnesses in the eye to discern whether they’re telling the truth. </p><p>“This is a bad process in place from an investigatory standpoint, from a research standpoint, from a how do you communicate it, how do you hold responsibility. There are a lot of pain points that we need to fix,” said Keicher.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bc0000" name="module-bc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. Not that he let on much. “Certainly one I wanted to get,” he said at the time.</p><p><b>Week 12. Thursday, Nov. 26 at Lions, noon (CBS 2)</b></p><p>The last time the Bears went to Ford Field they played the worst game of the Ben Johnson era. In Week 2 last year, they were beat 52-21. In their second game without Johnson, the Lions averaged a team-record 8.8 yards.</p><p><b>Week 13. Dec. 6 vs. Jaguars, noon (Fox 32)</b></p><p>Coach Liam Coen took a shot at Caleb Williams this offseason when he said his Jaguars got little respect but he sees “40 pictures of Caleb Williams” on the NFL’s web site each day.</p><p><b>Week 14. Dec. 13 at Dolphins, noon (CBS 2)</b></p><p>The Bears should handle the Dolphins. Johnson is familiar with their scheme — their head coach, quarterback and defensive coordinator were all with the Packers last year.</p><p><b>Week 15. Saturday, Dec. 19 at Bills, 7:20 p.m. (CBS 2)</b></p><p>In what should be the Bears’ Game of the Year (Non-Packers Edition), the team will face off against MVP favorite Josh Allen inside the Bills’ sparkling new stadium — and in prime time.</p><p><b>Week 16. Friday, Dec. 25 vs. Packers, noon (Netflix)</b></p><p>The Bears will wear their “Rivalries” uniform — orange helmet, navy jersey, orange pants — on Christmas day against the Packers. The Packers will wear their standard road uniforms.</p><p><b>Week 17. Jan. 3 vs. Lions, 3:25 p.m. (Fox 32)</b></p><p>Of every team all season, the Bears have the league’s best edge in rest between games, relative to their opponents, per Sharp Football Analysis. They’ll have three extra days’ rest than the Lions, who play Dec. 28.</p><p><b>Week 18. at Vikings (date, time, TV all to be determined)</b></p><p>The Bears and Vikings will have to wait for details of a game that might decide a playoff berth for either team.
